newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African life competition hotting up - Sanlam.
newsitem.headline: S.African life competition hotting up - Sanlam.

text.p: Competition is hotting up in the South African life assurance industry with foreign companies eyeing the market and local retailers moving into financial services, Sanlam managing director Desmond Smith said.
A total of 25 companies had made "firm inquiries" with the Financial Services Board, the industry watchdog, about setting up in South Africa, he told reporters on Tuesday at a results presentation.

Leading supermarket chain Pick 'n Pay Stores recently announced plans to move into financial services and Smith said other retailers where likely to follow suit, prompted by the success of Marks and Spencer in Britain.
"We also believe Richard Branson will be entering the South African financial services market in the not too distant future," Smith added.

Mutually-owned Sanlam recorded a 15 percent increase in consolidated income in the year to December 31 to 28.1 billion rand. But a 25 percent increase in policy benefits to 13.4 billion and higher taxation meant earnings for the capital portfolio fell to 1.6 billion from 2.1 billion.
"It wasn't an easy year... it was also a year of uncertainty," Smith said.
Premium income from individual business increased by a modest three percent to 12.2 billion.
"The main culprits were surrenders and other early terminations which are indicative of the pressure on the consumer as a result of inter alia economic uncertainties," he said.
Net investment income increased by 19.8 percent to 8.3 billion rand in 1996, although a weak South African stock market meant share returns were somewhat disappointing.

"But the 10.6 percent achieved by our investment team compares outstandingly with the 9.3 percent of the All Shares Index and also beats a basket of major competitors by more than a percentage point," Smith said.

For the current year, Smith said he was confident that the Johannesburg Stock Exchange would offer better value for investors in the second half. But the indications were that inflation over the next few years might be lower than over the past year or two.

"For the consumer this is good news, but combined with lower nominal interest rates, this will inevitably result in lower investment returns. This may force the industry -- not only Sanlam -- to reduce bonus rates."

On December 31, Sanlam's investment assets were distributed 58 percent in shares, 22 percent in public sector loans and stocks, 11 percent on other interest-bearing investments and nine percent in fixed property.
